utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There is no means to carry out an investigation about it? Maybe Mr. Harmon. Can I repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As far as the superiors of Mr. Erdemovic are concerned or the direct superiors, do you have any information concerning him and is there an investigation on the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: By virtue of the information provided to us by Mr. Erdemovic, we have the identifications of the some of the superiors and our investigation is focused on those individuals as well as others. As I mentioned previously, your Honour, our investigations are ongoing in relation to this event. They have not concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to supplement the question that my colleague asked you. We can state that we are somewhat surprised that Drazen Erdemovic is here before this Tribunal, because he himself confessed to the crimes that he committed, but since in the end you place a great deal of weight on his words, which we all do, we can in fact be surprised that there has not yet been an accusation or an indictment made against one of these people, for example, the head of execution squad. A little while ago I was speaking about the Lieutenant Colonel, but what about the other executives? We could go very up in the chain of command. It is natural for Erdemovic to be tried here, but you are putting a lot of weight on his words having to do with himself but we are surprised - I am now no more speaking about the Lieutenant Colonel about whom you gave us some evidence, but about the other people who were there. For example, the head of execution squad, he is identified, he is named and the Tribunal really has to ask the question. It is not at all, Mr. Prosecutor, being done in order to criticise the way you work in your office, but it is simply because we must try a man and, in order to try a man, he must be placed within the total scope of the events which took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to that, I believe that by virtue of the evidence that has been presented today we can certainly put Mr. Erdemovic and his role in these events and his relationship to other individuals in perspective. On the issue of when the Prosecutor's Office intends to issue indictments, obviously those are matters that are under discussion by the Prosecutor. I would prefer not addressing those publicly with the Court at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have noted your answer. I would now like to ask a question of Jean Rene Ruez. When you spoke about what had been said by the survivors, you said that the story of what had happened corroborated what Mr. Erdemovic has said. The question I would like to ask is the following. What is your feeling about the sincerity of Erdemovic's confession? Specifically, it has to do with the details or any additional details. Let me explain what I mean. You have said that this scenario was always the same. In the beginning, and you will excuse my euphemism, things were relatively organised. It is difficult to speak about organisation which is well put forward in something which is so grim, but after that happens everything goes wrong. Some of the people seem to enjoy hurting the prisoners who were there. This is what Erdemovic has told you, but I would like to ask you what your feeling about this is. Do you have the feeling that Erdemovic minimised his own role or an approximately correct description of what happened? This is very important when it has to do with the attenuating or mitigating circumstances which are the central point of this hearing. It is easy, of course, to say that the others were drinking, that the others were hitting people with iron bars, that I did not do it, I did the minimum. I know you do not have any proof about this, but what is the feeling you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do understand the essence of your questions. In order to answer it I would say that have having to do with the points in his statement, there were many which we were able to corroborate and the verification that we carried out was what led to the confirmation of the events as they took place as they have been described. The details of how these things were done, as you said, we have no way of investigating this in order to be sure that these have been correctly related. My opinion, and this is to the credit of Drazen Erdemovic, is that he volunteered to come to state the facts before this Tribunal. Likewise, he took the risk of identifying the perpetrators to lead to their arrest and that possibly one day they would hear their version of the facts. My personal point of view is that this approach, that is the way he describes his role in the events, makes what he says credible. I repeat that we are still investigating this. So long as we do not have access to other perpetrators and to their version of facts as they might relate them, we are not in a position in order to give a definitive judgment about this point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Therefore, you are only confirming what the Tribunal has already noted about the other participants. The Tribunal would like to have this information so it can do its work impartially. If there are no other questions, I think we can thank Mr. Ruez. Remain available to the Tribunal, please, because within another sequence in these hearings we will have the opportunity of speaking about attenuating or mitigating circumstances having to do with the co-operation of Erdemovic with the Office of the Prosecutor. You have already spoken about this to some extent and we will speak about it again. I thank now for what you have said. You can now go back to your office. Having to do with what is going to come next, the Tribunal has decided that it will hear Drazen Erdemovic before the Defence witnesses. Since it is now 12.30 we suggest that we should resume at 2.30 with the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic. For the time being the session has been adjourned. 12.30 p.m. (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Turning to the Registrar, would you please have the accused ushered in? I believe the photographers have finished. As the Tribunal announced at the end of this morning's session, the Tribunal has decided that it would hear as a witness Mr. Drazen Erdemovic. He will be listened to about the facts. The Trial Chamber will not at this time listen to anything about mitigating or attenuating circumstances which will be pleaded by his own lawyer or by the Prosecution. He can present the facts and the Judges, therefore, can see how the accused reacted to the facts which he is going to recount, and how they have been recorded both in the indictment and through the testimonies, either oral or in writing, those of Mr. Ruez and any anonymous witnesses who will be called to testify. Mr. Erdemovic, would you rise, please? Please take your place at the witness box. MR. DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, do you hear me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Since you are standing, would you please read the declaration which all witnesses must make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, please be seated. The Tribunal is going to ask you to recount the facts in which you played a part and for which you have been accused specifically with the charge of crime against humanity. After that, the Judges will ask you questions. There are questions which, if you do not wish to, you do not have to answer. The Tribunal will deduce from that what it will deduce but, for the time being, since you are testifying under oath, you will recount the acts, the acts for which you have been charged, before the International Criminal Tribunal. We give you the floor. Would you please tell us under what conditions you came about to be involved in the crimes which were committed at the farm where you found yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would first like to say that I did not wish to do that. It was - I was under orders. If I had not done that, my family would have been hurt and nothing would have been changed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to stop you right here. I would like you to answer what the Tribunal has asked you. We must understand one another. First of all, do you hear me? The Tribunal is not asking you to say that you did not want to commit the crimes for which you have been accused and for which you have appeared. You will be asked about those but, for the time being, the Judges are asking you to recount, to give us the story of the acts from the time that you were involved in this Sabotage Division until that moment when you left the farm complex, when you fired your last shot. Do you understand me? Do you hear me? Then, as far as the rest is concerned, your counsel will say it - we know that he will - you will say it, you will have the opportunity to say it and to prove it as well, but for this moment, for right now, we would like to know how you experienced and how you participated in these acts and, moreover, the Judges will ask you specific questions dealing with these acts. Did you understand what I said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have. I joined the 10th Sabotage Detachment approximately on 1st April 1994. Before that, together with my wife, I left Tuzla and came to Republika Srpska, more precisely, to Bijeljina on 3rd November '93. So from that day until April '94 I was not a member of the army of the Republika Srpska, although I was under an obligation to do so. I kept hiding in Serbia as long as I could and as long as me and my wife had enough money for that. When the money ran out, when problems started in Serbia and Republika Srpska and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I went back to my wife's uncle in Foca. When we arrived in Foca, and I am a Croat, I went to report my nationality. I went there to tell them the story how it came about that I ended up in Republika Srpska. They told me that my wife could stay in Foca because she is a Serbian. They told me that I should go back to Bijeljina because I had come there. They also told me that they could not guarantee my safety in Foca because there were only Serbs living there. So I asked my wife's uncle what it was all about, and he told me certain stories. I accepted that as a fact, so I had to leave Foca and go back to Bijeljina. When I arrived in Bijeljina, I went around, I went to the town hall. I went to register myself because the only document I had was my identification card which was issued in Tuzla. So when I got there, they immediately requested to see my papers, papers from my Unit, so that I could report myself to get some accommodation and everything else that I needed. There was a police raid that day in Bijeljina and I was with a friend of mine who is a Serb and the police approached us and they wanted to see our laisser passers, military passes. I did not have anything but, luckily, this man who was with me had some papers and he told me - he told them that I was a Croat from Tuzla, but I had helped many Serbs to leave Tuzla and reach the Republika Srpska. But they told me to go to the military department because I had no rights whatsoever because I was a Croat and I did not possess any document issued by the Republika Srpska. So, as I told Mr. Ruez, I went there alone. I was not taken there by the police. So I went to this military department and I told them everything that I have just told you. They presented me with two options: the 10th Sabotage Detachment, which had several Croats in it, one Slovenian and one Muslim. They also told me about another Unit, a Unit in which there were people who later on - who wanted to kill me when I went - when I left Tuzla. So I chose this other Unit. It was - it appeared more safe for me. I went to an interview with the Commander of that Unit and he asked certain Croats who had known me from before, he asked them about my character, and they told him that I was a good and honest person and that is how he admitted me to the Unit. So, I asked him what was the task of that - what was the mission of that Unit, and they told me it was mostly exclusively reconnaissance tasks. We were not securing any front lines. We did not - we were not doing other things, as the army of Republika Srpska. So I thought, and I said that to Mr. Ruez, that that was the only option for me and my wife who at that time was pregnant. I had nowhere else to go. Everything was all right with that Commander. We got along very well. He gave me the rank of sergeant, and while he was in charge I, unfortunately, saved only one life. It is the man who was given pseudonym X and who will testify I saved his life. So that Commander - I told him that story. I told him that I had saved one life and he said it was all right and he said that is what I should have done. After that, in October there was a change in the command and the Unit was extended. The Commander of our Unit became Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis. The relations were suddenly changed and certain nationalists amongst soldiers were becoming more important and only those people who thought as Pelemis were approved of. They did not think about honesty of other people and so on. So, as I said, I had a conflict with Pelemis after an operation that I refused. I was in charge of that group, I was its Commander and I was given an assignment. They provided me with all the necessary information and I left to carry out that task together with three other colleagues. They had to obey me because I was their Commander at the time. I was in charge and we had to go to the territory which was under the control of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I refused to carry out that task, because I told them that I had been given false information and that some civilians could get hurt, lots of civilians, both - and also that some soldiers, many soldiers of the army, of the Bosnian Army, could get killed and our soldiers as well. So that was the report that I submitted and my colleagues confirmed that report. They were very good people. On several days after from the main headquarters Colonel Petar Salapura arrived. He was the main intelligence officer in the headquarters. We were invited, myself and other Commanders who were there, and the meeting was mainly about my behaviour and the behaviour of certain other individuals. They told me that I was lying, that I could not behave that way, that I had let a prisoner go, that I had saved one prisoner's life (and that is the man who is going to testify today), that I was refusing orders and so on. That is when I was demoted. They took away my rank and I said, "OK, you think that I am lying, so please go and try to carry out that task", and that was all. My colleagues, other soldiers whom I think very good, from my group, they were very honest and I think they are grateful to me because I never ever allowed to expose them to some shady deals, difficult operations. After that, as I told you, problems started with Pelemis. I was being threatened, abused. There were all kinds of things happening. I do not remember all of them. So, as I told you, my rank was taken off, and then came the month of July when everything happened in Srebrenica, and I was assigned together with other soldiers - I was a simple soldier at that time - to go there. They did not tell us where we were going. They just told us to pack our things and to go. So when we arrived there, they told us, "You are in Srebrenica. Tomorrow you should get ready and you will be given assignments". So they told us some details. They just told us that, "It is probably going to be very tough", and so on. They also told us that Muslims were very extreme in that area and things like that. So the next day we set off. Yes, there was an order that we should not harm civilians, that soldiers should not harm civilians. So, as I could see it at that time, soldiers were not shooting at civilians who had surrendered. So we set off that morning and around 11 o'clock, 11.15 - I remember the hour because NATO planes bombed the artillery of the army of the Republika Srpska at that time - we entered the area with no resistance whatsoever, and I was surprised to see only maybe 100 of civilians in the town, only 100. So when we reached the centre of the town, they told us that everything was over and that we should stop and wait for the next command. Then Pelemis arrived. So he gathered us and he told me and four of my colleagues to go back and to report to him when Commander Mladic is coming to town. So that is what we did. We left to the southern area of Srebrenica. I did not know it was that area, but that was what Mr. Ruez explained to me when I got here. He told me that that was the southern part of the town. That day went smooth and, yes, I did see something. I did see when Pelemis ordered a soldier to kill a civilian who was approximately 30 years old. That was all I saw that day. The next day we spent the night in the southern part of the town, in a house, and the next day there was an order -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What day are you talking about, please, the events you have just outlined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 11th of July. So on 12th July we received an order - that is what Pelemis told us - to go back, that everything has been - that everything had been completed and that there was nothing else to do. So we went away in our vehicles, but our vehicle who was the last one in the column broke down and caught fire. That is why we were very late. We arrived in Vlasenica. There was a base in Vlasenica of the Vlasenica platoon and we learned when we got there that an APC had overturned and that a soldier was killed. Nothing really happened that day. It was already evening. We spent the night there, and the next morning when I got up I said that I would go to the funeral of that soldier who had got killed because he used to be in my group. So I went to his funeral. We buried this comrade and we came back to Vlasenica. The next day in the morning when we got up I got a new order. They told us that there was a task to be accomplished. The Commander of the group was Brano Gojkovic. I was a member of that group, a soldier, and seven other soldiers were also members of that group. We were told to report in Zvornik. Well, apparently, they told Brano where we were going, but I had no idea. So Brano reported to Lieutenant Colonel, to a headquarters with those military police units. So 10 minutes later this Lieutenant Colonel got out. He was in the company of two military policemen and he told our driver to follow his vehicle. The Lieutenant Colonel took us to a farm. I did not know the name of that farm. I just explained the location. I knew that the village of Pilica was there, but it was only when we got there that I learned what was happening. They told us that a bus load of civilians would come from Srebrenica. I said immediately that I did not want to take part in that and I said, "Are you normal? Do you know what you are doing?" But nobody listened to me and they told me, "If you do not wish to, if you - you can just go and stand in the line together with them. You can give us your rifle." I told you last time, if I had been alone, if I had not had my wife and a son, I would have fled and something else would have happened. I had to do that. I was forced to do that. Then buses started arriving. They took out people in groups of 10. They took them to the meadow. So we started shooting at those people. I do not know exactly. To be honest, I could not follow. It was simply I felt sick. I had a headache. I tried to avoid it as much as I could, try to avoid taking part in it. I wanted to save one man, but they would not let me. This man told me that he had helped many Serbs to leave Srebrenica and go to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So I knew that this man - I told them that this man had helped Serbs but that did not help. They told me, Brano told me that he did not want to have any witness to the crime. I kept silent and then a group of soldiers from Bratunac arrived and, as I told Mr. Ruez, they were just taking it out on those people. They beat them with iron bars. They cursed them. As for my group, nobody beat them with iron bars, but Stanka Savanovic, Brano were those who killed most of those people and Savanovic told us the reason why. He said that Muslims had killed his brother who had been 17 years old at that time. I do not know about Brano. After that, around 3 o'clock, I do not know the exact time, but I believe it was around 3.00 p.m., this Lieutenant Colonel came again together with those two military policemen and he told us that in the culture hall in Pilica there were, and that is what he said, that there were around 500 Muslim prisoners who were about to break out and flee. I said that I no longer wished to do it and then I am nobody's robot for killing. I just want to tell one more thing. If anyone had told me at that moment to kill that Lieutenant Colonel, I would have done so. Three of my colleagues stood by me and they refused to go. So they gave up the idea. However, those people from Bratunac went there. We heard some shots. We heard some explosions and Brano Gojkovic said that the Lieutenant Colonel had told us to come to a meeting, and the meeting was supposed to take place in a cafe across of the culture hall. I was not really paying attention to what the Lieutenant Colonel was saying. I was not interested at all. So, while I was there in that cafe, I was just listening to those shots and explosions. After that, after those people from Bratunac came to the cafe, the Lieutenant Colonel said that we were finished and that he wanted to talk to them alone. So, we got up and left. I said that I wanted to go home to see my child. That was it. So we went back to Vlasenica and in the evening we were bussed to Bijeljina. I got home. I wanted so much to see my child and my wife and when I got home I simply could not, I do not know, I cannot describe it. I could not sleep. Those days after that I started drinking. I just hated myself. I went out. I did not want to be at home. I was afraid to be home. I wanted to be among people. I just wanted to drink. My wife asked me what was happening with me and I said, "Nothing, nothing is happening". She noticed something. She knew because she had known me from before. I used to be very cheerful. I used to take her out down town together with my son. We used to go to a swimming pool which is in the vicinity of our home. I stopped doing all that. I do not know. I would spend only about two hours at home. After that something happened which I knew was going to happen. Kremenovic came to see me. I met with him and he told me that he had refused an assignment which was ordered by Pelemis and Salapura, and he told me he had had a conflict with them and Pelemis, apparently, told him that, "You and I will have to clear certain things and we will have to know who the Commander of the Unit is". So, on the next day, on 23rd July, there was a meeting about, concerning, orders that were issued by the command and concerning some other matters, something about us soldiers, soldiers of the Sabotage Detachment. But during the night of 22nd, as I said, I was down town. I had been drinking. That evening Savanovic, Stanko, who particularly enjoyed killing, shot at myself, Kremenovic and another colleague. I was hit by two bullets, one in my stomach and one in my lungs. I suffered very serious consequences. I had to undergo two operations of my stomach, two operations of my lungs on the left side of my chest. Kremenovic and this other friend sustained some minor injuries. I stayed one month in hospital, I do not know exactly how long, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Belgrade at the Military Academy Hospital. So when I went back to Bijeljina I went home. I knew what could happen to me. I told my wife to go back to her parents, to Tuzla, and to take our son with her. That is what happened. I managed at the very last moment to send my wife and my son to her parents and that is how I started my journey to The Hague, to tell what had happened to those miserable people. But when I gave an interview to a journalist of the NBC network, we were arrested in Yugoslavia. We were questioned there. They asked us why and how, and I told them, and I told the people from the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I told them how it all happened, how I was forced to do that, I had to do it. That is what I told the Court in Novi Sad and that is what I have told here and that is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Odio Benito, have you any questions you would like to ask? Examined by the Court

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Erdemovic, after being a member of the 10th Sabotage Unit, were you a member of other army or paramilitary groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Q. So this was your first experience as a soldier in Bosnia- Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I was in Tuzla, I was in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I was also in the HVO. These were regular units in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Why did you leave the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why did I leave the HVO? Because when I helped a group of Serb civilians, most of them were women and children, they arrested me. Soldiers from the HVO arrested me, and they beat me up and they harassed me as if I had killed the entire world. I helped women and children, that is why.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Women and children coming from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were from Dragunja, from my village. There were of Serb nationality and from the surroundings of Tuzla, because their husbands had left and gone to Republika Srpska beforehand and they left them there on the territory under Muslim control or Croat/Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you were beaten because you were helping Serb people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Being a member of this Sabotage Unit, did you receive any salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not regularly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you sign any contract to be a member of this army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think, I do not know exactly, but the authorities from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had that contract and my membership card, a card stating that I belonged to that Unit. I do not know if they sent it in with all my other papers. I do not know that exactly. It was taken away from me in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember who signed this contract between you and the Serbian Army, the name of the official who signed beside you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The contract was signed by Sergeant Pelemis (who was then a Sergeant) and General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember what this contract said in order to your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That contract said that I would be treated as a soldier until 1997. I do not know exactly what it said, but, how shall I put this, it is not that it had something to do or - how should I explain this - something that was against the law. It is not that there was something that was against international law or any other kind of law.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: At that time have you heard something about what happened in Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What were the missions this Sabotage Unit was asked to perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already said, reconnaissance in enemy territory, placing explosives in the artillery of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, also intelligence. That is part of reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Intelligence missions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember when you were in Pilica farm at what time did you start to shoot the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I think it was about 10 o'clock, 10.30. I do not know exactly. I think that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: At what time did you stop in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you, it was all completed, I mean, it all stopped at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, I think. I do not know exactly. Yes, 3 o'clock, but we did not take part in it until the end. The people came from Bratunac. That is what I told the people from - the gentlemen from the Prosecution. They were the ones who finished it. I do not know exactly when it stopped, but I think it was about 3 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many people were shooting at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the same time? I can tell, as far as my own people are concerned, the people I was with, eight people were shooting at the same time, eight of us, and I cannot say anything about the people from Bratunac because I do not know. I was not shooting with them. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What kind of weapon were you wearing or using?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally had an automatic rifle, kalashnikov, and some people had pistols, 7.62 millimetre calibre pistols.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you were using a kalashnikov rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know at the time of anyone who was shot for having disobeyed orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I will tell you, I am sure that I would have been killed had I refused to obey because I remember that Pelemis had already ordered one man to slaughter another man, and I am familiar with some other orders, I mean, what a Commander was entitled to do if he was disobeyed; he could order this person's liquidation immediately. I had seen quite a bit of that over those few days and it was quite clear to me what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many people did you kill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many people I killed, nor would I like to know how many people I killed, but I did tell Mrs. Vanessa Vasic Janekovic that I killed 70 people. That is what I told her and that is what I told the Court in Novi Sad, but I wish to tell you, it destroyed me, it killed me. I simply thought that my life was worthless after that. I lost everything I had. Finally, I lost my wife, my child. We parted. I just wanted the truth to be known and for someone to understand that this actually happened and how these people had lost their lives because, as we heard today, nobody knew about the place of Pilica, that a crime had happened there and what kind of a crime. Perhaps that is where most people were killed. To have someone believe me that I really had to do it, that I did not want to do it. That is why.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were they all men, young men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said - I told the investigator that I think - I do not know, I did not check - that they were from age 17 to 60, only men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, I would like to proceed with you chronologically, according to what you have been testifying. You went to Republika Srpska on 3rd November 1993. What did you do before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that I was at home and, as I said, before that I was in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the HVO was established in Tuzla, I was asked to join the military police of HVO. I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you changed sides several times. What forced you to go from the Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Croat military and then afterwards to go to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I did not want that. I did not wish to do so. I wanted to get away from the war as much as I possible. I went to the HVO because I was called upon to join the military police, because they stayed behind the front line and they were securing the control points, checkpoints, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You joined the military police, the Croat military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And yet you are a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But you also joined the Bosnia-Herzegovina and then you joined the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said under what circumstances, how I joined the army. I want to explain this. I did not want to fight a war. I could not leave Bosnia. I did not have a passport. I did not have anything, no papers, and I needed quite a few papers. First of all, in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina I was there because I was asked to join. I was mobilized and I did not commit any crimes, and I could never dream of what would happen to me in the Republika Srpska. I was in the HVO. I did not commit any crimes there. I did not do any harm to anybody. I did not go to Republika Srpska so that I would join the army. I went there a because a man, a Serb, had promised me; he has three sons in Switzerland, that he would transfer me to Switzerland, not that I would stay in Republika Srpska. As far as the army of Republika Srpska is concerned, I joined them six months after I got out. I got out on the 3rd November '93 and after six months, in April '94, I had to join the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you say you had to, you were forced to because you needed money or did they force you to join this Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not because of the money, because of my life. I did not have any documents. Careful, a Croat, I mean it is not important a Croat, but even a Serb, if he was not in the army of Republika Srpska, he did not have freedom of movement. He did not have anything, nothing. Where could I go? They could simply catch me in the street and say that I was a Croat spy and kill me without passing a verdict, nothing. Is it my fault that I tried to save my life - not only my own, but also of my wife and of my child? Am I to be blamed for that?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Please make clear, did you have any choice to go back to Croatia, to your country, or you were forced, you were urged to come into the 10th Unit of Sabotage? Did you have the choice to go back to your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, I told the distinguished lady Judge that I was beaten up by the Croats, not the Muslims, but the Croats because I helped the Serbs. So where could I go back to? To go back to get killed, right? I did not have any choice. Had I had a choice, I did not want to fight a war. I did not vote for any national party. I liked my life. I liked my comrades. I liked my friends. I lost different friends of various nationalities. I did not want any of that; all of that because of that Mafia that led us, all of us, the ordinary people, that led us into a war, and that is why I am testifying here today and that is what I am living for.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you chose to go into the 10th Sabotage Unit, were you aware of exactly the mission this Unit had? Was it known, was there a common knowledge about their mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. 100 per cent. I was 100 per cent aware of what the missions were and that is precisely why I decided to stay on in that Unit because it did not involve the loss of human lives. It involved artillery, old iron. That is why I stayed in that unit.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the beginning you refused to take action under Pelemis, I suppose he was your superior. The result was that you were degraded. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, Pelemis came in October and I was there from April '94 in that Unit and Pelemis came in October '94. The first Commander we had, I agreed with him. He saw that I was an honest man and that I was the only soldier who was married. I was the youngest soldier and I was the only one who was married and I was supposed to get a child soon. I was honest. First of all, I was not a nationalist. I did not hate anybody. I did not hate Muslims or Croats or Serbs. Honest people, but those who are dishonest I cannot like or love them. Of course I am not going to kill them, but I am going to say anything against them. When Pelemis came, that is when these things started taking place. I tell you now, I mean, some kind of orders that I did not like. They were related to the loss of human lives. That is it. That is why I had problems with Pelemis and not only me, but also others who agreed with me; Kremenovic also who was his deputy, he also had problems.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you were able to refuse the orders under Pelemis and then you mentioned also that after the executions in Pilica you also refused to go on and kill the 500 who were in this hall, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I wish to explain to you. I mean, my refusal of previous orders, I refused Pelemis's orders when I was the Commander and when I was the one who submitted reports, not when somebody else was the Commander, because when somebody else was the Commander I was not allowed to refuse orders because if I would create problems, then he would be killed immediately, and if I was in command, then I would reach agreement with these other people who were soldiers, and it is on those conditions that I refused an order of Pelemis's. The rest, you said that I refused to go to this public building. That is true, yes. I was fed up. I do not know. I cannot explain, describe, how I felt then. I had really had enough, and simply, as I said a few minutes ago, that this Lieutenant Colonel - had this Lieutenant Colonel said that we had to, I mean, I really would have killed him immediately and it would not matter what would happen to me after that. I said, "Was there not enough blood? Was there not enough dead people?" That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: My question is, you refused twice to execute the orders and you went out of it degraded at the maximum but not hurt. Why did you not also refuse to participate in the execution at Pilica farm? Was it any different? Was there more danger there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to apologise now, especially to the ladies present, and I will show you what I got because I refused this order in Pilica. Please, with your permission, I am going to show you this. (The witness pulled up his shirt). That is it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned after the cafe, after the day you went to the cafe, and you were shot there with other people, was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not only me, but those people who explicitly rebelled against Pelemis, those people, not only me, and not because of the drinking and the pub, but everyone knows why.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many people were chosen for the execution in Pilica farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight people.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did they choose you among them for any personal reason, for any special reason? Why were you selected among these eight people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Pelemis knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, I have a comment I would like to make first. I understand that it is painful for you, but you must know that you are before a Tribunal which must take into account a man who participated in the murder of dozens of people. All of us are accountable here. We understand that you were caught in a storm, but that is not a reason, neither because you pleaded guilty, nor because you are a person who carried out something as part of a great tragedy, for us just like that to say that these many, many people who were killed simply will be written off. This is what the Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber would like to recall here within the confines of these walls. We cannot only allow, simply because you recognise that, simply allow shadow areas in a file which will have great weight on your conscience over many years to come, but the conscience of the Judges is important as well. This is the comment which I wish to make first. I am not going to ask you many more questions, but I would like to ask you that if between 13th and 16th July, while you were on site in Srebrenica, did you have any news that you heard over the radio, either over the military radio or the radio from the headquarters, did you hear any news? You told us, Mr. Erdemovic, that during the 61 hearings against Messrs. Mladic and Karadzic that you yourself had recognised several facts, perhaps you had even seen General Mladic. I am asking my question again: do you know anything specific about what happened, anything with your comrades or other comrades in your Unit were saying that "We are killing Muslims", that "We are massacring Muslims". Are you aware of that? Were you aware of that? I would like you to be very specific in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know anything at any given moment between 13th and 16th July? You say that there was nobody in Srebrenica any more, but your Unit was there. There were other comrades, there were other groups there. You had heard at one point people saying, "We are killing Muslims, we are getting rid of the Muslims"? This is a very specific question I am asking you. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I will try to give you an answer as much as I can. First of all, I did not know. I told you, I was surprised when we entered Srebrenica that I did not see more than 100 people there. However, I realised many things here and through BBC, and I learned where people had been in the UN camp in Potocari, and I did not see that at the time and I do not know where Potocari exactly is. I did not know what was going on. Of course, I did not know - I do not see a reason why anybody from the command would tell me that Muslims were being killed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You yourself, did you not ask any questions? This was a safe area, a protected enclave. You knew that. It was a safe area and suddenly you are there and there is no one there. Did you not wonder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I kept asking myself what was going on. Of course. I told you, when we started they told us that there were civilians there, that there were some heavily armed extremists there, and when I realised that nobody was there, of course, I asked myself what was going on. I kept asking myself, "What is going on?"

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On the road, on the way to the farm, what did you see by the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Along the road, well, there were - all the way from Vlasenica to the vicinity of Zvornik soldiers were deployed along the road. They were securing the road and you could hear shots coming from the woods. That is what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you shot the people who were brought out of bus, let us be clear about this, you shot the people who were brought out of the buses. The Tribunal will judge as to the conditions, but the fact is that you killed those people. What were those people doing? Were they looking at you? Did they have their hands tied behind their backs? Were they dressed in civilian dress or were they wearing military clothes? Were you there when they were buried? Did you have the feeling there were any survivors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know how precise I can be. First of all, I was in a very bad emotional state. I do not know. It was horrible. It was so difficult for me, but I had no choice. I had no choice. Whether those people were looking at me, I do not know. I did not check whether they were dead.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were their hands tied behind their back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that on the first bus, and that is what I told in the investigation, some people had their hands tied behind their backs and they were blindfolded. I remember the first bus only. Mr. Ruez asked me whether there had been any other such people in other buses, and I told him I do not know and I cannot answer that question because such was my emotional state. I cannot explain that to you. It cannot be explained.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor about the person who said they would be getting you to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not give them any details. They did not ask me anything. If they had asked me for details, I would have given them. I can explain. I can provide them with all the necessary details, names, surnames, whereabouts, and they can check that the sons of that man live in Switzerland. I have no reason to lie. I cannot lie because of all those people who are dead.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before finishing, yes, a fellow Judge has a question. Just one second. I would like to turn to the Office of the Prosecutor: gentlemen, have any enquiries been made to check up on what the accused has said about this going to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been informed reading his statements and this general information with no certain facts that has not been pursued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about this incident in Croatia? That is very important because Mr. Erdemovic has told us that a lot of his behaviour in Srebrenica is related, as it were, to the fact that there was this promise that had been made that he would be going to Switzerland that did not work out, and then in Croatia he committed certain acts so that he could not return to Croatia. Mr. Ruez, perhaps if you deem it appropriate, you could have him come back, but did he look into that, whether there was some likelihood of truth in that, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When Mr. Ruez returns, I should propose that we ask him these questions. It is not known to me that he has been asked about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, your Honours, I am not from Croatia. I am from Bosnia and Herzegovina by origin. That is where I lived. I was a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not of the Republic of Croatia. I am from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry. Maybe I was not clear. I thought on the basis of what you said in response to Judge Riad's question that you could not return to Croatia because of an act you committed there. I did not quite understand the full implications.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to Croatia. He asked me whether I could go back home - that is how I understood him - back home to Tuzla where I am from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, I gathered from your answer to Judge Odio Benito that most of the victims or all the victims were Muslims, was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I do not know exactly. I did not check, but it was told that people were from Srebrenica. That is all.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said you tried to save some of them. You saved some?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I had tried to save one man, but I did not succeed because Brano Gojkovic said that he did not want to have any witness to that crime. He was the Commander of the Unit and he probably had received such an order from the Lieutenant Colonel. I do not know exactly, but I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you did not save anybody at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Brano Gojkovic was the Commander of the Unit and he decided on everything. I was just a regular soldier who carried out his orders.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But you tried to save him, you tried to save some?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did try. I thought I would succeed the way I managed to save the life of this person who will testify in my defence, but I was not successful in that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said you tried to save the life of the person who will testify, so you saved him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he was not in Srebrenica. It happened on the mountain of Majevica in the vicinity of Tuzla. He was not there in Srebrenica. I saved him in August 1994, I believe, one year before the events in Srebrenica, almost a year before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before concluding with the testimony of Mr. Erdemovic, you were called as a witness by the Tribunal. Now I would look at the Prosecution, look to the Defence, since this is a witness of the Tribunal, normally we would leave it at that, but should the Office of the Prosecutor have some questions, it may go ahead with them. But, if it does have some questions, then the Defence shall have the right to put questions as well. If Mr. Ruez should be called again, there again the Defence can raise some questions. If the Defence has questions, then of course the Prosecution can raise questions as well. Please proceed, Mr. Ostberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the opinion of the Prosecution, all relevant questions have been put by the Court so we have decided not to put any questions to Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you have any questions for Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in respect of the execution of the act and the facts you mentioned, I have no questions in relation to that. I think that the Court has covered everything that we needed to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Then there was one matter I would raise. There was a problem of checking whether an attempt had been made to check up on the two allegations made about going to Switzerland, on the one hand, and then, secondly, the action against Croats. Maybe we could hear Mr. Ruez again or, rather, by the end of the hearing, either today or tomorrow, would you be providing us with an explanation that might be read by the Registrar and that would go into the case file?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, we will try to do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. We are going to proceed to a recess. We shall resume at 4 p.m. (3.45 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing shall resume. Show in the accused. Office of the Prosecution, the Judges would like us to move on, first of all, hearing you and then the Defence. We would like to hear everything that can indicate how much co-operation you received from 8 the accused and also whether there might not be any aggravating circumstances. So, would you desire to call a witness on this score? Do let us know. I think tomorrow morning we will be able to listen to the Defence. There again there will be a possibility of producing witnesses and we will be hearing about anything relevant in the way of mitigating circumstances. I would recall that Mr. Drazen Erdemovic has pleaded mitigating circumstances while pleading guilty. You have the floor, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I would like to recall Jean Rene Ruez to the stand. I would like to inform the Court I will be calling him for two reasons. The first point, your Honour, is to answer the Court's concerns and questions about points raised by Mr. Erdemovic's testimony, specifically whether he informed the Office of the Prosecutor about his attempts to get to Switzerland and whether he also informed the Tribunal about the events relating to attempting to save people while he was a member of the HVO. After I have examined Mr. Ruez on that point briefly, then I will turn to the issue of Mr. Erdemovic's substantial co-operation with the Office of the Prosecutor. MR. JEAN RENE RUEZ, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jean Rene Ruez, we shall not have you make a solemn declaration again, but you are still under oath. Let that be clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Further examined by MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, during the course of your investigation into the events relating to Srebrenica, when did you first come into contact with the defendant in this case, Mr. Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first contact I had with the accused was just after his arrival on 24th April of this year.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On that occasion did he provide you with a statement relating to his knowledge of the events that he has testified about, today and previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I would like to focus on two brief points in his statement to you in April. Did he first of all ever inform you that he had tried to get to Switzerland, but that he had been unsuccessful in doing so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On that same occasion did he inform you that he had been a member of the HVO, that he had attempted to assist people cross the lines, but that he was arrested, beaten as a result of those efforts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. He said that he had helped a number of people to cross over to the Republika Srpska, that he was arrested by the Bosnian Muslim authorities and that he had been ill-treated by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber, Mr. Ruez, the circumstances of how Mr. Erdemovic arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at first, given his behaviour during the executions at the farm, Mr. Erdemovic indicated that he was afraid of retaliation against himself, primarily because of the fact that he was not all that co-operative during the executions. He also said there was an incident involving the leader of the group, the leader of the execution squad, in connection with the use of a machine gun, that people were merely being wounded and they were made to needlessly suffer. Now, the second thing he mentioned was his attempt to save the life of one of the prisoners. That did not work out because his group leader indicated that it was out of the question to leave any witnesses of that operation. Now, those views confirmed, according to him, since a few days later on the night of 22nd and 23rd July when he was in a bar, one of the members of the execution squad shot at him four times in a row wounding him seriously. He was helped by one of his mates and he could be evacuated to a hospital where he was given treatment, but subsequently heard about some rumours to the effect that people in his Unit were unhappy to hear that he had not been killed that night. He also made approaches to the Commanding Officer of his Unit to be given some help. For example, he wanted to buy some drugs but the help was refused by the head of the Unit. He also took advantage of the possibility to go to the Republic of Yugoslavia, to evacuate his wife and his child, to see to it that they could be brought to Tuzla and to safety. Thereafter, he made demarches to enter contact with the International Tribunal, which at the time there was not an office in Belgrade, which meant that via his comrades he was in touch with the press office that was in Belgrade at the time. Now, apparently, the press office was being monitored by the security service and his attempts gave rise to some suspicion. There was increased monitoring, and he was subsequently informed that the security services were aware that he was trying to make contact with the International Criminal Tribunal. Now, with regard to the statements Mr. Erdemovic wanted to make before the Tribunal, a few days prior to his arrest, were brought to the Office of the Prosecutor's attention. Now, this prior information allowed the Office of the Prosecutor to react quickly and to have him transferred quickly to The Hague. So it was at the Scheveningen prison that we had subsequent contacts on three occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, has Mr. Erdemovic provided substantial assistance to the Office of the Prosecutor in the conducts of its investigations relating to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he mentioned a number of events. In fact, he mentioned four specific events that we were not aware of at the time he brought them to our notice. The first two - these are the main two - were already mentioned earlier today - I mentioned them - these are the events that took place at the Branjevo farm and in the Pilica building. But there is also the fact that when on 11th July he was at Srebrenica, when the people remaining there were not putting up any resistance, the officer who was commanding his Unit gave the order to one of the members of the Unit to execute a Bosnian Muslim prisoner who was in the town. Now, that prisoner had his throat cut at the order of the Commanding Officer of his unit. Now, the second act: after he returned to Bijeljina on 13th - so this is on 13th - the same Commanding Officer gave an order to two soldiers in the presence of all the other members of the Unit to cut the throat of a prisoner who was used in reconnaissance missions by the unit. He had been taken prisoner by them three months before and was used for reconnaissance operations beyond enemy lines. He did not witness the execution, but the perpetrators did tell them that it took place and the individual had his throat cut in the woods near Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you have identified four events that Mr. Erdemovic informed you of in relation to what occurred in and around Srebrenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was the Office of the Prosecutor aware of any of those events prior to being so informed by Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. None of these events were known to the Office of the Prosecutor before Mr. Erdemovic told us about them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Erdemovic also provide you with the identities of perpetrators in relation to each of those four events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each time the identity of the perpetrators was known to Mr. Erdemovic, he told us their identity. The officer in charge of the Unit who ordered the murder, Srebrenica is Lieutenant Pelemis who is in charge of the 10th Sabotage Unit. The members of the execution group who were involved in the incidents on 16th at the farm, their names were also given by Mr. Erdemovic; the head of that group being Brano Gojkovic. The other members being Aleksandar Cvetkovic, Marko Boskic, Zoran Goranja, Stanko Savanovic, Vlastimir Golijan, Franc Kos, and he himself, Drazen Erdemovic. Now, the 10th Sabotage Unit was under the command of Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, before being provided with the names of those perpetrators, were you or the Prosecutor's Office aware of the identities of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not aware of any of these individuals at that point. With regard to the Pilica farm and the incidents there, Drazen Erdemovic also mentioned the very active part played by a group of individuals belonging to the Bratunac Brigade. Now, on his own initiative, while he was in his cell and he was watching television, he happened to see a BBC report about the events at Srebrenica, and while watching that film he recognised some individuals involved in the execution. We subsequently showed him the video of that film and he pinpointed one of the individuals that is seen in that film which is Brano Gojkovic. We now have a photograph of him. He also recognised one of the members of the Bratunac Brigade who was among the most active, so to speak, during the events. We do not know his name, but we do have a picture of him now, thanks to Drazen Erdemovic's help. Similarly, the general information he provided about the structure of his Unit and how it operated, these are very important, as I said, also in respect of the chain of command, because this Unit reports directly to the central command, so this Unit was under the direct command of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you please summarise the value of Mr. Erdemovic's co-operation to the Office of the Prosecutor's investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the information he provided us with was essential. I no longer here have with me Exhibit 1, that is to say, the map of the operations that ensued after the takeover of Srebrenica that we are acquainted with at this point. The main sites referred to by Drazen Erdemovic are those that are northern most on the map. Similarly, the number of the victims, when it comes to Branjevo, the massacre there, and the executions thereafter, in Pilica, given the number of victims, these are among the most major events that have been identified during our investigation. As I said, the number of sites, the distance given, this is something we consider crucial when it comes to seeing what was involved in terms of organisation, logistics, the command structure, preparation, planning, everything. You absolutely have to see what the level of responsibility of the overall aspect of the operation was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, as a result of your contacts with Mr. Erdemovic, have you been able to form an opinion as to whether or not he is remorseful for the crimes that he committed on 16th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Remorse, that is difficult really to specifically define. One thing is sure, however, and that is in the course of the contacts I have had with him he expressed his sincere regrets to being involved in that situation. He has always had a tough time saying how things happened during these events. Bringing all these memories together was something very difficult for him and always has been. On every occasion whenever he would go into details in the course of hearings, he would say how sorry he was to have participated in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Ruez, but I would like to tender to the Court the Exhibits that are items 1 through 15 of the book that has been presented previously. Exhibits 14 and 15 are transcripts of Mr. Erdemovic's testimony in the Rule 61 hearing that occurred in July of this year in relation to General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Registrar shall include that among the Exhibits. Judge Odio Benito, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Very briefly. Mr. Ruez, Mr. Erdemovic said he had helped a number of people to cross over to Republika Srpska. Did you identify any person who was helped by Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the investigation did not deal with that aspect of the events as described by Drazen Erdemovic. The investigation limited itself to developing the facts which followed the fall of the enclave, but that specific aspect was not at all developed during the investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you did not get any evidence of those activities of Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I would like to follow up on that question, the question that Judge Odio Benito asked. I suppose that what Mr. Erdemovic said was that he had been working with the Republika Srpska. Did he help people to pass to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He never spoke about that during our discussions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he say what type of people he helped to cross the border into Republika Srpska, Serbs Croats, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He gave only general information about that aspect during our interviews. At any rate, during our discussions at that point it was never gone into in any depth.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Erdemovic was arrested at the point that he was about to give information to the International Tribunal. That is what you said, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What are your sources for this? Did the press office there collect any information there about him that should be transmitted or was supposed to be transmitted to our Tribunal, or was this simply a question of chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the information was collated with one that had already been taken from a journalist who had been in contact with Drazen Erdemovic at that date.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: To whom he had already given information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to whom he had already given information based on which, even before the transfer of Erdemovic to The Hague, the investigation which had been announced to the press had already been announced. For example, at Pilica, what had happened at the Pilica farm had been pointed out and the first investigations had taken place at that point even before Mr. Erdemovic arrived at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he arrested for that reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason for his arrest was probably the quality of the information that he had to give, the gravity, the seriousness of the information which he was to transmit which had reached the knowledge of the police services and the judicial services of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which considered at that point appropriate to have him arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, going back to the beginning to the issue of Switzerland, the Swiss informant, we were not able to find out who this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. His statement on that point was merely to say that among the people who helped him to cross over into Republika Srpska, one of them had made a promise that he would help him and his wife to go to Switzerland if he were to cross the border into Republika Srpska, but once he arrived there that individual, allegedly, did not follow up on his promises. Therefore, he had to find a way to survive. Therefore, he joined the army which at that point seemed to be, according to recommendations which he had had, the only solution that he would have to survive, given the environment in which he was leaving at that point.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But on the two points of the men that he saved for which the Office of the Prosecutor does not have the specific information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we only based ourselves on his statements.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Therefore, you would agree with me that all of these mitigating circumstances which Mr. Babic will go into further are based on statements of Mr. Erdemovic himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For all of these - I cannot speak about all of the mitigating circumstances, but as far as the co-operation of the facts that he announced, we can say that the results of our investigation do show that he did not invent anything about those points. As far his own situation was concerned, that was not the purpose of our investigation and at this point we have based ourselves entirely on his own statements.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But his own situation as part of the two criteria which the Tribunal must use in order to come to a sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How do you interpret this turnabout of the Federal Republic Republic of Yugoslavia? He was arrested because he had given particularly reliable information. Is that why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I say that he was arrested at the point of his contacts when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was informed of the gravity of the acts in which he had been a participant and considered it appropriate at that point to arrest him immediately, without waiting any longer in order to find out what would be the follow-up for his own personal situation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A question I might ask the Prosecutor. How do you interpret this relative co-operation on the part of a country which we can say up to this point has not really demonstrated any strong desire to co-operate with the Tribunal? Do you have any idea about this question? Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have often asked myself the same question, your Honour, but I have been unable to answer the question and cannot answer the question today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea which would explain the turnabout that took place, because we could really call it a turnabout?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wish to say that the juridical organs in the Federal Republic Yugoslavia heard the accused Erdemovic, and they passed a decree after that to conduct an investigation and to start proceedings for a crime against civilian population from Article 142 of the penal code of Yugoslavia. Since I was the attorney of the accused Erdemovic on that occasion as well, I know that the highest state authorities decided that the accused Erdemovic should be sent to The Hague. As far as the motives for this decision are concerned, I cannot say anything. I can only say that the accused Erdemovic said loud and clear before the investigating judge of the court in Novi Sad that he wished to repeat all of that before this august Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will go on with the question. I do understand very well, and you have expressed it very well, that in Belgrade criminal proceedings were begun - no, in Novi Sad. Do you know if other procedures had been initiated against Erdemovic's superiors or did things stay at the level of Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the prosecution of the perpetrators of other criminal acts, before someone becomes accessible to the juridical organs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia they are not in charge before that, but since the accused Erdemovic came to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia then, according to the law, it was the port where he was apprehended that was in charge of pursuing proceedings against him. I imagine that other people were not accessible and not in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Secondly, criminal proceedings were started against not only Erdemovic but also Kremenovic whom he mentioned in his statement. True, not for a war crime against the civilian population, but also for hiding him as a perpetrator of such a grave crime and also for the illegal holding of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand, but I suppose that when the authorities of the Republic decided to respond positively to the request from the Tribunal, I think this is a question which must have been dealt with at a high level?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: At the highest level, decisions at the highest level. I believe that that decision was a new quality in the relations between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the International Tribunal for War Crimes committed in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Turning to the Prosecutor, I would like to ask you whether you intend - you spoke about co- operation, you spoke about remorse. I understand co-operation. I suppose that Erdemovic and his counsel will speak about his remorse. You did not speak about any possible aggravating circumstances. Should I therefore conclude along with my colleagues that you do not intend to raise the issue of aggravating circumstances in the commission of the crime recognised by the accused and in the way it was committed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the crime itself, the magnitude of the crime and Mr. Erdemovic's role in it, is an aggravating circumstance. This is a crime where there is evidence that hundreds of civilians, innocent civilians, were killed. Mr. Erdemovic at various times in various statements has admitted to killing between 10 and 100 civilians on this particular day. That, I believe, is a circumstance in aggravation, the magnitude of the crime and the defendant's role in it, that has been explained by Mr. Ruez and has been previously explained by Mr. Erdemovic as well. That will represent what, in the Prosecutor's view, are aggravating circumstances. We do not intend to present any additional evidence in regard to aggravating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There are no other questions? We will now suspend this hearing and we will resume tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock when we will give the floor to Mr. Babic to present all of the mitigating circumstances, because that was the line of defence which his client adopted. Perhaps we will have to hear Mr. Erdemovic again as a witness. Tomorrow I suppose, Mr. Babic, we will hear the two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question to Mr. Ruez, with your permission?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: When these statements were being made by Mr. Erdemovic, did he ever ask Mr. Ruez for something in terms of assistance, as an equivalent for giving such kind of statement? I think you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic never made any type of request at all. He always presented the facts, as we have tried to explain in more detail, as clearly as possible, with the best will possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Just a bit more. Mr. Ruez, did you make it seem likely to him that he would be treated favourably one way or another because he was saying all of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In no way. Since he was acting in a voluntary manner there was never any need to use any kind of artifice in order to get information from Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else? Would you like to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Court stands adjourned and we will resume at 10.00 in the morning tomorrow. I ask that the devices be put into place that are necessary for the protection of Witnesses X and Y.Thank you. 4.43 p.m. (The court adjourned until the following day).

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time) (4.00 p.m.)
